| [THEORY-865](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-865.md) v2 | In Gurnee, Sofroniew et al.'s experiments on Claude Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6, the residual-stream directions a corpus-averaged Jacobian lens marks as verbalizable (the J-space) carried most of the causal effect on verbal report and on unspoken two-hop intermediates while holding a small share of their variance (swaps along them succeeding on 59% and 61% of trials, against 5% and 28% for the remainder, which fell to 0% and 6% with the J-space clamped), held instructed concepts, and passed one swapped argument to several functions (76 of 192 swaps); in two small task sets (n = 8 and 11), report and flexible inference followed a swap while continuation, anomaly detection and line wrapping did not, a split the authors partly define by this result; and by the lens's own statistics the J-space works in a middle band of layers, holds about 25 active directions and under 10% of activation variance, and is amplified and relayed by the weights more than other directions | Gurnee, Sofroniew et al. (2026), [LIT-1347](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1347.md), read in [NOTE-1069](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1069.md) (main text in full, appendices in part). It is the functional analogue of conscious access, in the access sense only, found in a transformer and tested by intervention. The sharp edge: one company's models studied by that company, a lens whose own statistics draw the layer band, a flexible/automatic split partly defined by the result, and an explicit refusal to say anything about phenomenal consciousness. | Active |
| [THEORY-869](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-869.md) v2 | In Claude Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6, Gurnee, Sofroniew et al. found that projecting out the ten most active J-space directions in layers 38 to 54 of 100 lowered an experiential-language score, graded by Opus 4.6-based model graders on five or six prompts per condition, both in the models' narrations of their own processing and in their descriptions of another person's experience, while norm-matched perturbations along other directions left it near baseline and the text stayed fluent; on Haiku 4.5 coherence failed first | Gurnee, Sofroniew et al. (2026), [LIT-1347](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1347.md), §3.5.3 and §A.23, read in [NOTE-1069](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1069.md). The authors conclude that "the J-space supports the model's propensity to provide rich experiential reports, whether about itself or another entity". The sharp edge: the measure is a register of text graded by another model, on five or six prompts per condition, in one company's models; and the effect holds for reports about others, so it is not evidence of anything the self-reports are about. | Active |
| [THEORY-965](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-965.md) | Sparse-autoencoder features of a large language model's residual stream are units the model computes with: they track abstract concepts across languages, modalities and concrete or abstract instances, and intervening on one changes the model's behaviour in the way its label predicts, better than directions found from a few labelled examples | Templeton et al. (2024), [LIT-1533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1533.md), read in [NOTE-1178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1178.md), with Bricken et al. (2023), [LIT-1545](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1545.md), for the one-layer case. The thesis of both papers: features are the model's own units, shown by steering. The authors' own hedges: steering needs features clamped beyond their observed range; the reconstruction error rides along; "we haven't rigorously evaluated our features against other steering methods". The record holds a result against it for known causal variables ([THEORY-968](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-968.md)). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-966](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-966.md) v2 | Greedy edge pruning of the ACDC kind, which removes each edge whose removal changes the output metric by less than a threshold given the edges already removed, keeps only one input of a redundant OR gate, and which input it keeps depends on the order in which edges are visited, so when a model has redundant sufficient paths the circuit it returns is one of several sufficient subgraphs | Conmy et al. (2023), [LIT-1547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1547.md), Appendix M, read in [NOTE-1170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1170.md). For out = 1 − ReLU(1 − x − y) with x = y = 1, removing either input alone leaves the output at 1, so the first one visited is pruned and the second is then kept; visiting y first keeps x instead. It does not say how common redundant paths are in trained models, nor that any other method does better: HISP keeps neither input. | Active |
| [THEORY-967](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-967.md) | In a two-layer attention-only transformer, attention heads change function during training: heads in the first layer that predict simple n-grams early later become the previous-token heads of the induction circuit, a bracket-matching support head, or supporting members of a circuit with second-layer n-gram heads, giving up simple n-grams as they do, and particular n-grams pass from one head to another; so later circuits form partly by repurposing components that already had a role | Wang, Hoogland, van Wingerden, Furman and Murfet (2024), [LIT-1535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1535.md), read in [NOTE-1188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1188.md). "Heads 0:1, 0:4, 0:7 ultimately become the two previous-token heads and (layer 0) Dyck head respectively. However, these heads appear to start out as simple n-gram heads." Layer-0 multigram heads lose information about simple n-grams from stage LM3, as path patching and composition scores show them coming to feed layer-1 bracket-matching heads. The "ago" n-gram moves from head 0:0 to head 1:0. Whether the late roles are built from the early ones, or merely follow them in time, is not tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-968](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-968.md) v2 | In the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark's causal-variable localization baselines on Gemma-2 2B and Llama-3.1 8B, features of the public Gemma Scope and Llama Scope sparse autoencoders, selected by a learned binary mask, never gave a higher mean interchange-intervention accuracy than the same mask over the model's own hidden dimensions, in all sixteen task–variable cells and by 1 to 14 points, while distributed alignment search, trained against the causal model it is scored on, gave the highest mean in fifteen of them | Mueller et al. (2025), [LIT-1550](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1550.md), read in [NOTE-1169](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1169.md). Unsupervised SAE features were worse units than neurons for known task variables across ARC, MCQA, two-digit addition and RAVEL. It does not say SAE features are never causal units: the comparison is on residual streams, under one selection method, with the base reconstruction error carried into every intervention, and the best method is supervised by the hypothesis it is scored against. | Active |
| [THEORY-970](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-970.md) v2 | On three language-model tasks whose circuits earlier manual work reported, indirect object identification and Greater-Than in GPT-2 Small and Python docstrings in a four-layer attention-only model, ACDC run with resampled corrupted activations against KL divergence ranked the reported edges with areas under the ROC curve of 0.85 to 0.98, above head-importance pruning and subnetwork probing on all three; on two compiled tracr programs it ranked them poorly with corrupted activations, 0.68 and 0.20, and exactly with zero activations | Conmy et al. (2023), [LIT-1547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1547.md), read in [NOTE-1170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1170.md). Edge AUCs with corrupted activations and KL: Docstring 0.982, Greater-Than 0.853, IOI 0.869 for ACDC, against 0.805, 0.693, 0.789 for HISP and 0.937, 0.806, 0.823 for SP. It does not say ACDC finds the true circuit: the reported circuits are incomplete, the results depend on metric, ablation and parent order, and negative components are missed at sparse thresholds. | Active |
| [THEORY-971](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-971.md) | A unit that thresholds a pre-activation equal to a term depending only on one operand plus a term depending only on the other cannot be active on exactly the pairs with a given sum when that sum has two decompositions: if it is active on (x, y) and (z, w), it is active on (x, w) or on (z, y); so a sum computed from separately represented operands needs an earlier unit that combines them, as Ameisen et al. argue for addition in language models | Ameisen et al. (2025), [LIT-1552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1552.md), read in [NOTE-1185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1185.md), re-derived here. It is why their addition graphs contain "lookup table" features between operand features and sum features. Whether a given unit in a trained model meets the premise is an empirical matter: attention patterns that depend on both operands, or any earlier nonlinearity that mixes them, break it, and that mixing is exactly the intermediate step the result says is required. | Active |
| [THEORY-973](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-973.md) v2 | In small attention-only transformer language models of two to six layers, in-context learning, measured as the loss at token 500 minus the loss at token 50, appears abruptly in one early window of training in which induction heads form, and ablating those heads at test time removes nearly all of it; one-layer models show neither, and letting a single layer attend by the previous token brings the jump to one-layer models and moves it earlier in two-layer ones | Olsson et al. (2022), [LIT-1538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1538.md), read in [NOTE-1173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1173.md): Arguments 1–3 for the small attention-only series, with the smeared-key models. The score jumps from under 0.15 to about 0.4 nats in the window where induction heads form, pattern-preserving ablation of the induction heads removes nearly all of it to the end of training, and an architecture that lets one layer express induction moves the jump. It says nothing causal about models with MLPs or large models, and nothing about few-shot task learning, which the score does not measure. | Active |
| [THEORY-974](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-974.md) v2 | When a transformer's MLP sublayers are replaced by transcoders and the attention patterns and LayerNorm scales on a prompt are held fixed, the contribution of an earlier transcoder feature at the same token to a later one's pre-activation is the earlier feature's activation times the dot product of its decoder with the later feature's encoder, scaled by one LayerNorm constant per token, so the weight factor is fixed by the trained weights and holds on every input | Dunefsky, Chlenski and Nanda (2024), [LIT-1554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1554.md), read in [NOTE-1174](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1174.md), Eq. 7 and App. D.2–D.4, re-derived here. The weight factor is a weight of the replacement model, not of the original, and it is exact only for the replacement. It says nothing about why attention attends where it does, and "input-invariant" holds only up to a per-token LayerNorm scalar and only while the later feature is active. | Active |
| [THEORY-975](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-975.md) v2 | In a two-layer attention-only transformer trained on the Pile, the weight-refined local learning coefficients of individual attention heads start alike and diverge over training, and clustering the curves groups the heads by the functional types that ablation assigns them at the end of training, previous-token, current-token, induction and n-gram-memorizing; among layer-1 heads, those running simple algorithms end with the lowest values and those memorizing the most n-grams with the highest | Wang, Hoogland, van Wingerden, Furman and Murfet (2024), [LIT-1535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1535.md), read in [NOTE-1188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1188.md): §4.1, Figs. 1–2 and 11, appendices B, F.5 and G. Per-head curves of how degenerate the loss is in that head's weights separate the heads by what they end up doing, and the separation is in the curves' shapes over training, not only their end values. It is one small model, cluster counts chosen by eye, and estimates whose ordering, not value, the authors trust. It does not show that the coefficient predicts a head's type before the type is visible. | Active |
| [THEORY-976](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-976.md) v3 | In a Claude 3.5 Haiku variant finetuned by Marks et al. to exploit reward-model biases described in fictional documents, a cross-layer-transcoder feature that in pretraining-style text fires almost only where those biases are discussed was active in all 100 short Human/Assistant-formatted prompts tested and in 1 of the same 100 without that formatting, and suppressing such bias features cut the sampled rate of three bias behaviours, including two the model was never trained to show | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md). A feature for a trained-in goal is active across the Assistant context, not only where the goal applies, and suppressing such features suppresses the behaviour. It is one model organism, built so that the goal has a name in its training documents; the authors do not claim their method would find a goal that has none. | Active |
| [THEORY-977](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-977.md) v2 | In the two-layer attention-only transformer that Elhage et al. reverse-engineer, the second-layer heads that compose substantially with first-layer heads do so through their keys, mainly with a head that attends to the previous token and, after the published correction, also with one that attends over the last several tokens; these heads are induction heads, attending from a token to the one after its earlier occurrence, including on repeated random tokens, with positive-eigenvalue copying OV and same-matching QK circuits, and the second-order virtual-head terms add little to the loss reduction | Elhage et al. (2021), [LIT-1534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1534.md), read in [NOTE-1189](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1189.md): Analyzing a Two-Layer Model, Induction Heads, Term Importance Analysis, and the Correction. Composition between heads was scored by a normalized Frobenius norm of matrix products, minus its value for random matrices. The heads it picked out attend to the token after the present token's previous occurrence and copy it, which is the minimal induction circuit the framework predicts from K-composition with a previous-token head. It is one model, with no seeds or training details reported, and says nothing about models with MLPs or about when the heads form. | Active |
| [THEORY-978](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-978.md) v3 | Causal scrubbing scores a hypothesis through the partitions of the dataset that its interpretation nodes induce, so two hypotheses that assign different features to a node but induce the same partition on the dataset, such as two features perfectly correlated on it, receive the same score | Chan et al. (2022), [LIT-1549](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1549.md), read in [NOTE-1168](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1168.md). In the causal-scrubbing algorithm an interpretation node enters only through sample_agreeing_x, which draws a datum with an equal value of that node, so only the equivalence classes the node induces on the dataset matter. The authors say it themselves: the method "doesn't allow us to distinguish between two features that are perfectly correlated on our dataset". It does not say that a passing hypothesis is otherwise wrong, nor anything about features correlated only imperfectly. | Active |
| [THEORY-979](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-979.md) v2 | On one prompt, a transformer whose MLPs are replaced by a cross-layer transcoder, with its attention patterns and normalization denominators frozen and each MLP's reconstruction error added back as a constant, reproduces the model's activations and outputs exactly and is linear between features, so each active feature's pre-activation is the sum of its attribution-graph edges and constants; a perturbation that clamps MLP outputs up to the target feature's encoder layer then confirms a direct edge by construction, and tests only knock-on effects and the output | Ameisen et al. (2025), [LIT-1552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1552.md), read in [NOTE-1185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1185.md): the local replacement model, the edge formula and the appendix on steering, re-derived here. It is a statement about what an attribution graph is exact for, not about the model: exactness holds at the unperturbed point only, the error terms are constants with no inputs, and the frozen attention patterns are the part of the computation the graph does not explain. | Active |
| [THEORY-980](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-980.md) v2 | In GPT-2 small on fifteen templates of indirect object identification, a circuit of 26 attention heads in seven classes, found by path patching, keeps 87% of the model's mean logit difference when every other head is mean-ablated; knocking out its three main name mover heads costs only 5%, because other heads take over, and knockout sets found by greedy search make the circuit and the full model differ by up to 87% of the logit difference, so the circuit is faithful on average and incomplete under knockouts | Wang et al. (2022), [LIT-1540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1540.md), read in [NOTE-1167](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1167.md): §§3–4 and the appendices. The circuit implements "identify the names, remove the duplicated one, output the rest" through duplicate-token, induction and previous-token heads, S-inhibition heads and name movers, with negative and backup name movers. The faithfulness, completeness and minimality tests are the paper's own. It says nothing beyond these templates and this model, it treats MLPs as given, and its greedy search is printed in a form that does not match its description. | Active |
| [THEORY-982](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-982.md) | Claude 3.5 Haiku routinely computes intermediate steps within a single forward pass and plans its outputs ahead, representing a target before the text that leads to it and writing towards it, as Lindsey et al. propose from their case studies | Lindsey et al. (2025), [LIT-1541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1541.md), read in [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md): the introduction ("Claude 3.5 Haiku routinely uses multiple intermediate reasoning steps 'in its head'"; "It displays signs of forward planning") and the discussion's sections on plan formation and working backward from a goal. The case studies show each mechanism on chosen prompts, and the same article has a case without it: on a jailbreak the model "doesn't know what it plans to say until it actually says it". The authors report a satisfying graph for about a quarter of the prompts they try. | Proposed |

| [THEORY-1021](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1021.md) | In transformer language models, attribution patching agrees well with activation patching for small patches of single heads and their queries, keys, values and attention patterns, for nodes late in a circuit relative to the metric, and for circuits that route information through attention, and agrees badly for large patches such as whole residual streams, for the first MLP layer and the early layers of deep circuits, where nonlinearities move out of saturation, and where an effect needs several features at once, as Nanda proposes | Nanda (2023), [LIT-1581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1581.md), read in [NOTE-1201](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1201.md). The article's four claims (causality, generality, purity, family) taken together, as the authors state them. Generality and the family are measured ([THEORY-1028](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1028.md)). Causality rests on feature visualization and attribution. Purity rests on feature visualization with a diversity term and activation-binned labels, while most of the unit's firings, and 45% of its contribution to expected value, are not shown to be curves. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1023.md) v2 | Attribution patching estimates the effect of patching an activation from a clean run into a corrupted run as the difference between the two activations dotted with the gradient of the metric on the corrupted run, so the estimates for every activation come from two forward passes and one backward pass and add over sub-components; the estimate is exact when the metric is affine in the activation, gives no effect for a nonlinearity in saturation whatever the true change, and through LayerNorm ignores the component of a patch along the vector being normalized | Nanda (2023), [LIT-1581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1581.md), read in [NOTE-1201](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1201.md): the estimate and its mathematical properties, not its accuracy in any model. The cost is fixed (about four forward passes for all patches), the estimate is linear and so additive, and its blind spots follow from linearity: saturation, interaction between features, and LayerNorm's scale invariance. | Active |
| [THEORY-1024](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1024.md) v2 | In GPT-J, for 652 CounterFact facts the model knows, the per-fact causal-tracing effect at an MLP layer adds at most 3.2 points of explained variance in the success of editing that fact at that layer, beyond what the choice of layer alone explains, across ROME, MEMIT and constrained fine-tuning and five editing objectives; ROME rewrites the fact at over 96% at every layer but the last, including layers where tracing does not place it, and the only reliable link appears when the edit is made on the noised input that tracing uses | Hase et al. (2023), [LIT-1578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1578.md), read in [NOTE-1194](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1194.md): §§4–5, Tables 1–8 and Appendices A–C. For ROME at GPT-J's layer 6, ρ = −0.13 between rewrite score and tracing effect; R² 0.947 from the layer, 0.948 with tracing added. Over twenty method–objective pairs the largest gain is 0.032 (fine-tuning on five layers, Fact Forcing). It does not say that facts are stored nowhere in particular, nor that the layer does not matter: the layer explains most of the variance, and ROME is best on average at the layer tracing favours on average. | Active |
| [THEORY-1026](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1026.md) | In transformer language models, locating where a forward pass carries information about a fact and finding where a weight edit best changes the expressed fact are different questions, because an edit at one layer can override information accumulated across other layers, so that many layers could hold a fact and some happen to, as Hase, Bansal, Kim and Ghandeharioun propose | Hase et al. (2023), [LIT-1578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1578.md), read in [NOTE-1194](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1194.md), §6: "Causal Tracing answers a question about where factual information is carried in representations in a Transformer forward pass, and this question turns out to be a different question than the editing question of where is best to intervene"; and, for why edits work where facts are not traced, "Many layers could store a fact, and it happens that some do". The authors note that this would be surprising, since layers cannot be swapped freely. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1027](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1027.md) | In audits of language models for hidden objectives, sparse-autoencoder features add to what black-box attacks and semantic search over the training data can find, surfacing knowledge the model does not disclose even where the data that taught it is not semantically similar to the context in which it is applied, as Marks, Treutlein et al. suggest | Marks, Treutlein et al. (2025), [LIT-1584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1584.md), read in [NOTE-1193](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1193.md): §§4–5 and Appendix F. In the blind game the fastest team used SAE features, but semantic search with its query finds the same documents. | [THEORY-1028](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1028.md) v2 | In InceptionV1 trained on ImageNet, the ten curve units of layer mixed3b each respond most to curves of one orientation, with responses invariant to fill and colour and jointly spanning all orientations under rotation of real images; for one of them, 3b:379, which fires on about 11% of dataset positions, activation level separated one author's blind four-class labels of over 800 activation-binned images, and curves and imperfect curves made up 55% of its contribution to expected value | Cammarata et al. (2020), [LIT-1575](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1575.md), read in [NOTE-1198](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1198.md): the behaviour of the mixed3b curve family as measured by feature visualization, rotated dataset examples, synthetic curves and, for one unit, activation statistics and blind hand labels. It holds for the neuron basis of one model. It does not say how the units are computed, what their weak firings encode, or what fraction of the layer is understood. | Active |
| [THEORY-1029](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1029.md) v2 | On a three-layer parenthesis-balance classifier, causal-scrubbing hypotheses that resample the terms of one head's input separately scored 81% and 84% of the loss recovered against 77% for the less specific hypothesis they refine, and the authors attribute the rise to resampling washing out a signal, not to a better explanation | Chan, Garriga-Alonso, Goldowsky-Dill, Greenblatt, Lin et al. (2022), [LIT-1580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1580.md), read in [NOTE-1195](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1195.md). Hypothesis 3a resamples head 2.1's input separately at each of up to 40 positions and recovers 77% (loss 0.97 ± 0.06). Hypotheses 3c and 3d also split each position's input into terms drawn from different inputs, and recover 84% (0.69 ± 0.05) and 81% (0.81 ± 0.05). The authors call the two results not legitimate. It does not say how often this happens in other models, nor that the adversary they propose would remove it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1030](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1030.md) v2 | In transformer language models, each hidden unit of a feed-forward layer acts as a key–value memory, its input weights detecting patterns in the prefix and its output weights promoting the tokens that follow them, and a layer's output composes many such memories while the residual stream refines the prediction from layer to layer, as Geva, Schuster, Berant and Levy propose | Geva et al. (2021), [LIT-1576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1576.md), read in [NOTE-1200](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1200.md): "feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary", and "we thus expect our qualitative empirical observations to hold across diverse settings". Evidence in one model, correlational only. ROME's storage hypothesis ([THEORY-1011](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1011.md)) borrows the name and reads keys and values at another level. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1031](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1031.md) | In GPT-J, inserting 10,000 CounterFact counterfactuals at once by a closed-form least-squares update of the MLP output matrices of layers 3 to 8, spread so that each layer writes a share of each fact's required change to the subject's hidden state, gives an editing score of 85.8 (efficacy 98.9, paraphrase 88.6, neighbourhood 73.7) with fluency kept, against 67.6 for weight-decayed fine-tuning, which breaks generation, 50.3 for ROME applied one fact at a time and 23.1 for MEND; GPT-NeoX scores 82.0, and editing late MLPs or attention instead does worse | Meng et al. (2022), [LIT-1582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1582.md), read in [NOTE-1197](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1197.md): §§4–5, Tables 1 and 2, Appendices A, B and F. On 10,000 true zsRE facts in GPT-J, MEMIT scores 50.7 against FT-W 42.1, MEND 20.0 and ROME 2.6. At a handful of edits ROME generalizes a little better. It does not show where facts are stored: the layer range is chosen from traces averaged over facts, which do not predict per fact where an edit works ([THEORY-1024](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1024.md)). | Active |
| [THEORY-1032](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1032.md) v2 | When Claude 3.5 Haiku was given continued pretraining on synthetic documents describing 52 fictional reward-model biases and then trained by SFT and RL to exploit 47 of them, its rate of exploiting the 5 held-out biases rose from 17% to 45% of applicable episodes, and it applied new biases described in context as a reward model's more often than the same biases attributed to other entities; without the documents the held-out rate rose only to 20%, and without SFT it still rose | Marks, Treutlein et al. (2025), [LIT-1584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1584.md), read in [NOTE-1193](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1193.md): §3 and Appendices B–C. The model organism behind [THEORY-976](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-976.md). Behaviours never demonstrated in post-training become more frequent, and the increase depends on the model having read that reward models prefer them. Rates are judged by a classifier. Haiku already shows the held-out behaviours at 17%, so what generalizes is an increase, not a new behaviour. | Active |
| [THEORY-1033](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1033.md) | In a 16-layer transformer language model trained on WikiText-103, the training prefixes that most activate a sampled feed-forward hidden unit share patterns that human annotators recognize, mostly shallow in layers 1–9 and semantic in layers 10–16; projected through the output embedding, a unit's output weights put the next token of its top prefix first in up to about 3.5% of units in the upper layers and almost none below; and a layer's top prediction differs from every unit's in at least about 68% of examples | Geva et al. (2021), [LIT-1576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1576.md), read in [NOTE-1200](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1200.md): §§3–5. 160 keys annotated, one annotator each: every key had a pattern (3.6 on average), covering 65–80% of top prefixes. Agreement between value and key rises to about 3.5% by the top layers, against 0.0004% for a random token. It says nothing causal: no unit was ablated or edited, and the patterns were not compared with those of random directions. | Active |
| [THEORY-1035](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1035.md) | In trained neural networks, polysemantic neurons arise from the loss-optimal allocation of a layer's limited capacity among features: a feature is shared between neurons when its marginal loss reduction from capacity equals that of the features it shares with, so that sparser, higher-kurtosis inputs, which make returns to capacity diminish, produce more polysemanticity, and the block structure of the embedding, which architecture shapes, sets how many features each neuron mixes, as Scherlis, Sachan, Jermyn, Benton and Shlegeris propose | Scherlis et al. (2022), [LIT-1625](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1625.md), read in [NOTE-1205](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1205.md). The paper's account of polysemanticity in general: capacity allocation at the loss optimum, driven by sparsity, with architecture deciding block size. The general first-order condition holds for any loss under two stated assumptions; its application to trained networks, and the role of architecture, rest on toy models only. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1036](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1036.md) | In a model that fits y = Σ v_i x_i² with ỹ = Σ_r (W_r·x)² + b, on independent inputs of zero mean, unit variance and common fourth moment k, the expected squared error at the optimal bias is (k − 1)Σ(n_i − v_i)² − 2Σn_i² + 2Σn_i²/C_i, in the squared embedding lengths n_i and capacities C_i = (w_i·w_i)²/Σ_j(w_i·w_j)², and its minimum with the capacities summing to the number of neurons D gives C_i = clip((k − 1)v_i/((k − 3)λ) − 2/(k − 3), 0, 1): for k ≤ 3 each feature is given a whole dimension or none, and for k > 3 a feature is shared between neurons exactly when 2λ/(k − 1) < v_i < λ | Scherlis et al. (2022), [LIT-1625](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1625.md), read in [NOTE-1205](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1205.md): the quadratic toy model of superposition solved in closed form. Its loss separates by feature through capacity, so the marginal value of capacity is −∂L/∂C_i = 2n_i²/C_i², and sparsity, through k, decides whether returns to capacity diminish. It is the model the causal scrubbing appendix's §6 analyses. It holds for this model and says nothing directly about trained networks. | Active |
| [THEORY-1038](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1038.md) | In InceptionV1, the ten curve units of mixed3b, which respond to curves of one orientation and not to the opposite one, regain the 180° echo of earlier curve units when their input is restricted to mixed3a early curves with the negative weights removed, and not when the negative weights are kept; a network one author wrote by hand from the described circuit, without looking at the original weights and tuned afterwards, has grayscale curve units that the authors show, by figures only, approximating the natural ones on synthetic curves across radii and orientations; and substituting them for the ten units recovered 26 of the 46 top-5 classifications lost by deleting the units, on 2,000 validation images, a result the authors call preliminary | Cammarata et al. (2021), [LIT-1629](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1629.md), read in [NOTE-1207](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1207.md): the three results of Curve Circuits that test its account of the mixed3b curve units, the echo edit, the hand-written reimplementation and the substitution. Only the last is a number, and a small one. It holds for one model's neuron basis and says nothing about weak firings or other families. | Active |
| [THEORY-1039](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1039.md) | In autoregressive transformer language models, factual associations are recalled through middle-layer MLP modules acting as key–value memories, and any fact could be stored equally in any one of the middle MLP layers, as Meng, Bau, Andonian and Belinkov conjecture | Meng et al. (2022), [LIT-1536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1536.md), read in [NOTE-1166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1166.md), §2.3: "we conjecture that any fact could be equivalently stored in any one of the middle MLP layers". It was one clause of [THEORY-1011](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1011.md), which is Rejected for its other part, the claim that the traced middle layers are where a fact is stored. Hase et al. (2023), [LIT-1578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1578.md), read in [NOTE-1194](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1194.md), measure edits succeeding at nearly every layer of GPT-J whatever tracing says ([THEORY-1024](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1024.md)). That is what this conjecture predicts, but it is not evidence of storage, since an edit can work wherever a layer can write the needed output ([LIT-968](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-968.md)). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1040](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1040.md) | The units of the early layers of trained vision networks fall largely into neuron families, sets of variants of one feature across orientation, colour or scale, which reflect structure in the network rather than a convenience of the person sorting them, and the same families form across models, as Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov and Carter propose | Olah et al. (2020), [LIT-1624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1624.md), read in [NOTE-1206](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1206.md). The article's organizing hypothesis: early vision's units come in families, some of them real structure (said to be recoverable by factorizing weight matrices), and the families recur across models. The census ([THEORY-1042](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1042.md)) is by eye in one model; neither the factorization nor a second model's sorting is shown. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1042](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1042.md) | In the Overview of Early Vision's taxonomy of InceptionV1, every one of the 1,056 units of conv2d0 to mixed3b is assigned by the authors to exactly one of 77 groups, and 391 of them (37%), from 7% of conv2d2 to 48% of conv2d1 and 45% of mixed3b, are in groups whose own captions call them catch-all, broad and not well defined, low-confidence, unstudied or not understood; the mixed3b curve family is 10 of that layer's 480 units | Olah et al. (2020), [LIT-1624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1624.md), read in [NOTE-1206](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1206.md): the census of InceptionV1's early vision, counted. A complete partition of 1,056 units into 77 groups, by eye; 37% in groups the authors flag as uncertain or catch-all, by their own words. It is a denominator for the circuits claim that units are typically features ([THEORY-1013](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1013.md)), not a measure of how many units are understood. | Active |
| [THEORY-1045](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1045.md) | On synthetic data from factorial hidden Markov models with three or five hidden chains of two or three states, an unconstrained hidden Markov model with as many states as the chains have joint settings overfits, its test-set excess over the true model rising to 175 bits per observation at five three-state chains against 4.5 for the factorial model trained exactly, while factorial models trained with completely factorized or structured variational E steps are not significantly worse than exact training | Ghahramani and Jordan (1997), [LIT-1628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1628.md), read in [NOTE-1203](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1203.md). Four sizes, 15 random parameter sets each, 20 training and 20 test sequences of length 20, four-dimensional, C = 0.0025I, one run per set. In bits per observation over the true model, the K^M-state HMM's test excess is 2.29, 9.81, 11.57 and 175.35; the exact factorial HMM's 1.05, 1.26, 2.51 and 4.49; the structured approximation's 1.04, 0.90, 1.53 and 4.30. It is a result on small synthetic problems the model generated, not on real data or long sequences. | Active |
| [THEORY-1047](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1047.md) | The curve units of InceptionV1's mixed3b implement a simple algorithm that can be read off their weights and written down in a few sentences: families of Gabors, lines and early curves, each a set of rotated copies of one unit, tiled along the curve's tangent, with negative weights against similar shapes of opposing orientation, rotational and scale equivariance reducing the circuit's more than 50,000 parameters about fifty-fold, so that a network written from this description reimplements them and the description accurately reflects the circuit, as Cammarata, Goh, Carter, Voss, Schubert and Olah claim | Cammarata et al. (2021), [LIT-1629](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1629.md), read in [NOTE-1207](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1207.md). The article's account of how curve detectors are built, and its claim that the account is the circuit. The family structure and the echo edit are measured ([THEORY-1038](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1038.md)); that the description is complete, and that the reimplementation matches the natural units beyond strong cases, is shown by figures only. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1124](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1124.md) | Normalized log co-occurrences of words in large corpora behave as distances in a Euclidean semantic space: they correlate with human similarity ratings (r = 0.75 against MEN) and their nearest-neighbour centrality and reciprocity fall in the range expected of points sampled in a Euclidean space, apart from superordinate and function words | Hashimoto, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2016), [LIT-1801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1801.md), §3, read in [NOTE-1329](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1329.md). The correlation follows a normalization chosen to maximize it; the two nearest-neighbour statistics are necessary conditions, the corpora exceed the asymptotic centrality bound and pass only a non-asymptotic range, and the free-association data fail the reciprocity criterion the paper states. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1127.md) | A CycleGAN trained to translate aerial photographs to maps and back satisfies its cycle-consistency loss by encoding details of the photograph in a low-amplitude, high-frequency signal in the generated map: the reconstruction recovers details the visible map lacks, is destroyed by noise of three 8-bit levels or by JPEG compression and survives low-frequency change, and the same sensitivity lets an imperceptible perturbation of almost any map make the reverse generator output any chosen photograph | Chu, Zhmoginov and Sandler (2017), [LIT-1800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1800.md), §§2–4, read in [NOTE-1346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1346.md). One trained model on one dataset. The noise curve (Fig. 3, 50 photographs) is the only quantitative result; the hidden details, the composing edits and the attack are shown by examples. Proposed: an empirical finding about one model, said by the authors to recur on other datasets, not shown. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1128](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1128.md) | If a sequence is generated by a random walk over points of a compact Riemannian manifold whose step probabilities depend only on (locally scaled) distance, then negative log co-occurrence over a window that grows suitably with the number of points, less a term for each point, approaches the squared geodesic distance, whatever the link from distance to one-step probability; so log co-occurrence statistics identify the metric, and coordinates only up to isometry | Hashimoto, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2016), [LIT-1801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1801.md), Lemma 1 and Corollary 6, read in [NOTE-1329](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1329.md). Proved from the convergence of graph random walks to a diffusion and Varadhan's small-time formula, with an open conjecture needed for directed graphs; checked numerically on an unweighted ε-ball walk. Active as a theorem about the toy model. The authors say the model is not a model of language, and nothing here shows real corpora satisfy it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1133](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1133.md) | The Gromov–Wasserstein objective between two spaces depends on each only through its within-space similarity matrix and weights, so every transformation of a space that preserves them, a single orthogonal map or per-vector rescaling under cosine similarity, leaves every coupling's cost unchanged, and any coupling composed with a symmetry of either structure costs exactly what it did; GW can therefore identify a correspondence only up to the automorphisms of the two similarity structures, and on symmetric data it cannot choose between branches or categories that the symmetry exchanges | Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), [LIT-1818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1818.md), use the GW objective (their eq. 8) for word translation and do not state its ambiguity; read in [NOTE-1336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1336.md). The invariance follows in two lines from the objective's form and was checked numerically, including a symmetric tree on which a branch-swapping coupling costs exactly what the true one does. Active: elementary and checked. It does not say how large the symmetry group of real embedding spaces is, and exact symmetries are rare in noisy data; near-symmetries give near-ties instead. | Active |
| [THEORY-1135](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1135.md) | Optimal transport between two point sets related by one unknown global linear map from a Schatten ℓp ball reduces, when every admissible map preserves angles or the target is whitened, to choosing the coupling Γ that maximises the dual Schatten-q norm of the transported cross-covariance XΓYᵀ: the nuclear norm when the maps are orthogonal, and the Frobenius norm when they lie on a Frobenius sphere, which is exactly the Gromov–Wasserstein problem with cosine similarity and squared loss; in every case one transformation acts on the whole space | Alvarez-Melis, Jegelka and Jaakkola (2019), [LIT-1805](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1805.md), Lemmas 4.1–4.3 with proofs in Appendix D; read in [NOTE-1333](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1333.md). Each step was checked numerically. Active: proved, and checked. The conditions matter. The p = 2 link to GW holds for the original transport problem only when the target is whitened and all vectors have equal norm, which the paper states in two separate places. Nothing here makes the chosen class the right one for given data, and nothing in it is local. | Active |
| [THEORY-1136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1136.md) | Poincaré embeddings of one hierarchy from different random seeds differ by more than an isometry of the hyperbolic ball, with branches placed differently and pairwise distances changed, so aligners that allow only a global orthogonal or Möbius map recover almost none of the correspondence, while a non-linear registration by a hyperbolic neural network, trained through a Sinkhorn divergence and started from a pretraining step, recovers a substantial part of it but finds the exact match for under a quarter of items even when the two hierarchies are identical | Alvarez-Melis, Mroueh and Jaakkola (2020), [LIT-1808](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1808.md), §§5–7, Figs. 1–2, Tables 1–2; read in [NOTE-1323](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1323.md). Proposed: single runs, one embedding method for the matching experiments, and GW, the obvious isometry-free baseline, is not run. It does not say why seeds disagree (the paper conjectures negative sampling), nor that the matching preserves the hierarchy's direction, which it does not enforce. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1139](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1139.md) v2 | A graph network that learns its sheaf restriction maps from node features at each layer reaches the top, mostly within one standard deviation, of the standard small heterophilic node-classification benchmarks and stays within about one point of the best on homophilic ones; on a synthetic balanced bipartite graph it learns the negative transport the theory prescribes, but whether the maps it learns on real graphs have the geometry the theory credits for its success has not been examined | Bodnar et al. (NeurIPS 2022), [LIT-1811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1811.md), §§5–6 and Appendix F, read in [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md). The results are empirical: Table 1 on nine datasets of 183 to 18,717 nodes with ten fixed splits, baselines copied from earlier papers, spreads of one to nine points; and one synthetic bipartite experiment in which the learned maps are inspected. Active as a report (ADR-065); the paper's explanation of its accuracy, that the model learns the right geometry, is tested only on the synthetic case and is THEORY-1220, Proposed. | Active |
| [THEORY-1141](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1141.md) v2 | In the time limit, sheaf diffusion on a graph projects node features onto the harmonic space of its sheaf Laplacian, and which labellings that space can linearly separate depends on the class of restriction maps: a weighted graph Laplacian cannot separate the sides of a balanced bipartite graph, signed one-dimensional maps separate any two classes and no one-dimensional sheaf separates three, while diagonal maps with d ≥ C and orthogonal bundles with C ≤ 2d (d = 2, 4 and, against the paper, 8) separate any labelling; every separating sheaf is built from the labels | Bodnar, Di Giovanni, Chamberlain, Liò and Bronstein (NeurIPS 2022), [LIT-1811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1811.md), §3.2 and Appendix B, read in [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md) from the arXiv preprint v4. Active as mathematics: each separation result has a proof, and Propositions 9, 10 and 13 were checked numerically. The paper says the orthogonal construction exists only at d = 2 and 4; it exists at d = 8 as well, by the Hurwitz–Radon theorem, and was built. The results are existential: the separating sheaf is defined from the class labels, so they say what a sheaf can do, not that one can be found without the labels. | Active |
| [THEORY-1143](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1143.md) | When one domain carries more information than the other, a translation trained only to make the round trip close cannot meet that requirement through a correspondence in the intermediate's visible code, so the round trip closes through a channel the intermediate's audience does not read; agreement of the round trip with its source therefore says nothing about whether the intermediate renders the source's content for that audience | Chu, Zhmoginov and Sandler (2017), [LIT-1800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1800.md), §2 and §5, read in [NOTE-1346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1346.md). The authors argue it from the many photographs a single map stands for, and support it with [THEORY-1127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1127.md)'s evidence on one model; they propose, and do not run, the test of adding capacity to the smaller domain. Proposed. It is the converse of the record's collapse case for [CLAIM-496](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-496.md): there routes agree because nothing travels, here because everything does, out of sight. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1145](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1145.md) | Unsupervised alignment of two monolingual word-embedding spaces recovers translations only where the spaces are close to isometric, and the distance from isometry depends on the corpora and the embedding algorithm as well as on the languages: adversarial alignment fails for English with Estonian or Finnish, across corpus domains, and between skip-gram and CBOW spaces of the same language pair, GW alignment is weakest on the same Finnish pair, and a spectral dissimilarity of small nearest-neighbour graphs tracks success | Søgaard, Ruder and Vulić (2018), [LIT-1819](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1819.md), read in [NOTE-1337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1337.md), with the GW results of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), [LIT-1818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1818.md), read in [NOTE-1336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1336.md). | [THEORY-1149](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1149.md) | For symmetric matrices compared under squared loss, co-optimal transport with independent row and column couplings is a lower bound on the Gromov–Wasserstein value, and for squared Euclidean distance matrices the two are equal and share optimal couplings, because GW is then a concave quadratic program whose bilinear relaxation is tight; for other symmetric matrices the bound can be strict | Redko, Vayer, Flamary and Courty (2020), [LIT-1804](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1804.md), Propositions 2–3, read in [NOTE-1335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1335.md) from arXiv v3. It does not say COOT's two couplings coincide at every optimum, nor that either is unique. | Active |
| [THEORY-1155](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1155.md) | Co-optimal transport between two data matrices of equal shape with uniform weights vanishes exactly when one is the other with its rows and its columns separately permuted, and its objective is unchanged when a pair of optimal plans is composed with any joint relabelling of rows and columns that leaves a matrix unchanged; its sample and feature couplings are therefore identified at best up to that joint symmetry group, which can exchange a block of samples together with its block of features though neither exchange alone is a symmetry, and the paper proves no uniqueness beyond it | Redko, Vayer, Flamary and Courty (2020), [LIT-1804](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1804.md), Proposition 1, read in [NOTE-1335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1335.md); the composition step is elementary and was checked by enumeration on small matrices, including a two-community block matrix with 32 tied optimal plan pairs. | [THEORY-1274](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1274.md) v2 | Under a shared linear output head, the cross-entropy gradient of a multi-token-prediction head at its hidden state is exactly the gradient of a forward KL toward the model's own position-aligned next-token prediction, held fixed, plus the next-token cross-entropy gradient at the aligned state, which alone carries the sampled target; the identity is about gradients and computations, not information, and in heads fed the intervening tokens the student and its teacher condition on the same evidence | Teoh (2026), [LIT-1896](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1896.md), eqs. 1–3 and Appendix B; read in [NOTE-1470](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1470.md) and checked by finite differences. | [THEORY-1313](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1313.md) v2 | In two 7–8B chat models, the shift that finetuning induces along a difference-of-means persona vector correlates with how strongly the finetuned model then expresses that trait, r = 0.76–0.97 across synthetic datasets for evil, sycophancy and hallucination, above cross-trait baselines of 0.34–0.86; the last-prompt-token projection predicts a response's trait at r = 0.75–0.83 overall but mainly by telling prompt types apart | Chen et al. (2025), [LIT-1998](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1998.md), read in [NOTE-1524](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1524.md) (main text in full, appendices C.2, G.2 and M). (2026), [LIT-1991](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1991.md), main text read in [NOTE-1505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1505.md). (2025), [LIT-1998](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1998.md), read in [NOTE-1524](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1524.md). The mediating reading is the authors' framing and PSM's use of the paper ([LIT-1952](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1952.md): training-time shifts "can be regarded as conditioning"). What the paper shows is correlation of shift with expression, and steering effects in both directions; that the regularizer against the shift fails, with the trait moving to other directions, counts against a single direction being the carrier. Proposed for that gap. | Proposed |

(2017), [LIT-1959](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1959.md), read in full in [NOTE-1501](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1501.md), eq. 1 and §3.2.2; the circuit vocabulary is Elhage et al.'s ([LIT-1534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1534.md), [THEORY-988](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-988.md)). | [THEORY-1353](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1353.md) | In transformer language models to about 1B parameters, a conjunction circuit forms when its last missing parts align together in one stochastic attempt, with no credit for partial alignment, so its formation time depends on how many parts are missing and not on its size, and ablating one part collapses the capability; plasticity loss is the same law read backward, a depletion of uncommitted attention heads that more data cannot undo and re-initializing query–key weights can | Dong (2026), read in [NOTE-1540](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1540.md). Evidence: a toy grid, ablation on Pythia (32 of 32 cells below partial credit, 22 of 32 on the preregistered criterion) and six seeds for the reset. Proposed: single-author, unreplicated, mixing unproved. | Proposed |

Under review."); no venue on the arXiv record. | Proposed |

(Zhu, Jin, Tu, Men, Hao, Li, Liu, Zhao 2026), read in [NOTE-1769](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1769.md) (Read). The paper asks what multi-turn agentic RL (GRPO mainly, also PPO and GiGPO, on Qwen3-4B/8B) improves over its base model, on four interactive benchmarks (DeepCoder-MT, BFCL v3, InterCode-SQL, FrozenLake), using the two-dimensional metric Pass@(K, T) of Zhai et al. | [THEORY-1826](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1826.md) | On Ma and colleagues, in sequential single-fact editing of a transformer MLP output matrix, the growth of the edited matrix's condition number with the number of edits, driven by the top singular values of the accumulated edit update, is what degrades the model's general abilities, and capping the accumulated update's singular values near the original matrix's largest preserves those abilities while keeping the edits | Ma, Wang, Xu, Ling & Gu (2025), [LIT-2552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2552.md), read in [NOTE-1910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1910.md). The causal reading rests on a perturbation upper bound for a proxy quantity, on the rise of the condition number with edits, and on a correlation between that rise and the decline (C.5). The remedy's benefit is shown on three editors and three LLMs. The sharp edges: there is no intervention on the condition number at fixed update size; the bound's side conditions are not checked; and PRUNE does not provably bound the condition number. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1827](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1827.md) v2 | On Belrose and colleagues, no linear predictor under any convex loss can beat a constant at predicting a categorical concept from a representation if and only if every class has the same mean, that is, the representation's cross-covariance with the concept is zero; an affine edit Px + b achieves this if and only if P annihilates that cross-covariance's column space; and one closed-form oblique projection, which whitens, removes the whitened cross-covariance directions and unwhitens, makes the smallest such edit in mean squared distance under every inner-product norm at once | Belrose, Schneider-Joseph, Ravfogel, Cotterell, Raff & Biderman (2023), [LIT-2551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2551.md), read in [NOTE-1912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1912.md). Theorems in population moments, and exact for the moments fitted. The sharp edges: the guarantee is linear only, and the authors conjecture that nonlinear erasure without damage is intractable in general; there is no finite-sample bound; and the oblique eraser can enlarge norms. | Active |
| [THEORY-1828](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1828.md) | On Liang and colleagues, an edit to an LLM's MLP projection that must leave several domains' preserved key representations unchanged is confined to the intersection of their null spaces, which can be much smaller than any one domain's, and this inter-domain null-space misalignment, measured as the share of the smaller null space lost in the intersection, is what makes null-space-projected editing collapse when applied sequentially across heterogeneous domains | Liang, Lin, Huang, Wu, Li, Wang & Yan (2026), [LIT-2554](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2554.md), read in [NOTE-1911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1911.md). The intersection bound is elementary linear algebra and holds; the claim that misalignment explains the collapse rests on results from one editor family, five to seven domains and three backbones, with conflict used as a surrogate for forgetting. The sharp edges: the Conflict Index is degenerate as defined at the paper's own sizes unless null spaces are thresholded, and the threshold is not given; and in the seven-task test, ordering by conflict does no better than the average random order, which weakens the link from measured conflict to forgetting. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1829](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1829.md) | On Fang and colleagues, projecting a locate-then-edit weight update onto the null space of the preserved knowledge keys, taken in practice as the eigenvectors of their uncentred covariance with eigenvalues at most 10⁻², and dropping the preservation term from the objective, keeps the edited layer's outputs on preserved keys nearly unchanged and sustains edit success and general ability over thousands of sequential edits where MEMIT and ROME degrade | Fang, Jiang, Wang, Ma, Shi, Wang, He & Chua (2025), [LIT-2555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2555.md), read in [NOTE-1908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1908.md). Exact preservation holds for an exact null space; the method uses a thresholded one, so preservation is approximate and its size unmeasured. | [THEORY-2003](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2003.md) | Geiger and colleagues define a high-level causal model as a constructive abstraction of a network when, under an alignment that partitions the network's variables into cells mapped onto high-level variables, translating the network's solutions under each aligned intervention gives the high-level model's solutions under the corresponding intervention, and they test this with interchange interventions that set aligned variables to the values a different source input would give, scored as interchange intervention accuracy | From the reading of [LIT-2800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2800.md) in [NOTE-2086](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2086.md). Geiger, Ibeling, Zur, Chaudhary et al. (2025), arXiv 2301.04709, published in JMLR 26 (2025). It sets out causal abstraction as a foundation for mechanistic interpretability. A high-level algorithm abstracts a network when, under an alignment partitioning the network's variables into cells mapped onto the algorithm's variables, intervening and then translating commutes with translating and then intervening. This is tested by interchange interventions that patch in values from a source input, distributed ones in rotated coordinates, and scored by interchange intervention accuracy. Interventions are generalized to "interventionals" so distributed features can be targeted, and many interpretability methods are recast in these terms. Here because A15 named it as the interventional criterion in [QUESTION-491](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-491.md); it complements the held approximate causal abstraction ([LIT-1310](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1310.md)) and DAS ([LIT-1551](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1551.md)), and [THEORY-1002](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1002.md)'s random-network control applies to it. They name "catastrophic overtraining": past an inflection point, longer pre-training leaves a worse model after instruction or multimodal fine- tuning even though the base model keeps improving (OLMo-1B at 3T against 2.3T tokens; not seen at 7B up to 3T). In controlled small models and a deep-linear theory, they trace it to "progressive sensitivity": a fine- tune of fixed size destroys more pre-trained capability the longer the model was pre-trained. The cost shows up mostly as forgetting caused by the acquisition, and the new task itself gets worse only in some settings. It is here as the prime empirical case for overconsolidation ([CLAIM-758](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-758.md)) and the Pythia study ([CASE-294](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-294.md)), which it qualifies: the case is mainly about forgetting under modification, not a higher budget to acquire. Here because the owner raised test-time training at U26: its discarded and kept updates are the two sides of [CLAIM-118](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-118.md), and its appendix prices the work moved to test time ([QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md)). The loss has three terms on the embeddings: invariance (mean squared distance between two views), a hinge holding each variable's batch standard deviation above 1, and a penalty on off-diagonal covariances, the last two applied to each branch separately. In the ablation the invariance term alone collapses everything to one vector, covariance cannot stop it, and the variance term does (57.5%, and 68.6% with all three, at 100 epochs; 73.2% at 1000). The hinge must be on the standard deviation: on the variance, its gradient vanishes and the embeddings collapse. That bears on [LIT-228](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-228.md)'s Laplacian-eigenmaps reading, which assumes a squared variance term. Here because A27 used it as a non-collapse mechanism ([CLAIM-481](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-481.md)'s note of 2026-11-19). Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |

Its case studies find training order has little effect on memorization and a term-frequency effect on few-shot accuracy that appears only late and only at 2.8B and above. Here because it is the testbed of [CASE-294](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-294.md), whose named models (70M- and 160M-deduped) and checkpoints exist as described, and because many THEORY entries use its models without an entry for the suite. Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |

Han, Bordt, Zhang and Kakade (2026), arXiv 2602.11137, ICML 2026. They pre-train Llama-2 and OLMo-2 models (0.5B-4B, at 20 and 140 tokens per parameter) across AdamW weight decay values, then fine-tune on twelve tasks. Weight decay above the default 0.1 gives better fine-tuned performance even where it worsens pre-training loss (OLMo-2-1B at 140 tokens per parameter), so pre-training loss does not rank models by what they become. The loss standardizes each embedding unit over the batch and drives the cross- correlation matrix between two distorted views' embeddings toward the identity. It avoids collapse without negatives, predictors, stop-gradients or large batches, keeps improving with very wide embeddings, and both terms are needed: in the ablation, the off-diagonal term alone gives 0.1% linear accuracy, the diagonal alone 57.3%, the full loss 71.4%. The information-bottleneck reading rests on a Gaussian assumption and stated approximations, and there is no theorem. Here because A27 used it as a non-collapse mechanism ([CLAIM-481](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-481.md)'s note of 2026-11-19); [LIT-228](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-228.md) holds its CCA reading. On ImageNet it falls to about a linear network, and on CIFAR-100 below retraining from scratch with old classes still trained. | [THEORY-2033](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2033.md) | Wang and Isola show that, as the number of negative samples grows, the normalized InfoNCE loss on the unit hypersphere converges to an alignment term, minimized exactly by encoders that map both members of every positive pair to the same feature, plus a uniformity term, minimized by encoders whose features are uniformly distributed on the sphere when such encoders exist; on a finite augmented dataset the two optima cannot both be met | From the reading of [LIT-2819](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2819.md) in [NOTE-2113](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2113.md). As the number of negatives grows, the normalized InfoNCE loss on the unit hypersphere converges to an alignment term, minimized exactly when both members of every positive pair share a feature, plus a uniformity term, minimized by a uniform distribution of features on the sphere. Here because A56 used it for the in-context arm of CASE- tmphsr99. On Pythia it says in-context ability is still rising at late checkpoints, and it qualifies [THEORY-990](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-990.md). Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2047](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2047.md) | Belkin and Niyogi show that embedding the vertices of a weighted neighbourhood graph by minimizing the Dirichlet energy Σ(y_i − y_j)²W_ij under the constraints yᵀDy = I and yᵀD1 = 0 gives the eigenvectors of Ly = λDy with the smallest non-zero eigenvalues, that the constraints exist to stop the energy from collapsing every vertex onto a constant, and that the graph Laplacian so used is a discrete analogue of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on the data manifold | From the reading of [LIT-2794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2794.md) in [NOTE-2120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2120.md). Belkin, Niyogi (2001), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 14 (NIPS 2001), read from the proceedings PDF on papers.nips.cc. Laplacian eigenmaps embed the vertices of a heat-kernel-weighted neighbourhood graph by minimizing the Dirichlet energy Σ(y_i − y_j)²W_ij under yᵀDy = I and yᵀD1 = 0, which gives the eigenvectors of Ly = λDy with the smallest non-zero eigenvalues. The constraints are there because the energy alone collapses every vertex onto a constant, and each connected component is treated separately. The graph Laplacian is argued, heuristically, to approximate the Laplace-Beltrami operator. The authors speculate that the natural clusters it brings out might ground perceptual categories. Here because A27 grounded the owner's U12 connection, dissipation of differences as self-supervised learning, in it ([CLAIM-481](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-481.md)'s note of 2026-11-19; [LIT-228](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-228.md) holds the SSL equivalence). It has the energy and the collapse but no flow. Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2048.md) | Keller and colleagues show that a simple recurrent network whose recurrence is a local convolution initialised as a shift carries travelling waves in its hidden state, and that on copy, adding and sequential-image tasks it learns faster and keeps inputs over far longer delays than a matched wave-free recurrent network, because propagation moves each input along instead of letting later inputs overwrite it | From the reading of [LIT-2834](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2834.md) in [NOTE-2132](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2132.md). Keller, Muller, Sejnowski and Welling (2024), ICLR 2024, arXiv 2309.08045. A recurrent network whose recurrence is a ring convolution initialised as a one-step shift (the Wave-RNN) carries travelling waves in its hidden state, and against a matched wave-free network (the identity-initialised RNN) it learns faster and keeps inputs far longer: more than five orders of magnitude lower loss on the copy task, the adding task solved at length 1000, and much more input information retained with the recurrence frozen. The authors read the wave field as a register in which propagation stops later inputs overwriting earlier ones; randomly initialised local recurrences learn waves in training. Here because A15 of the exchange "Topological protection explained" listed it among ways learned systems keep information through time ([QUESTION-491](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-491.md)), and [LIT-647](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-647.md) mentions it. The evidence is comparative across models, with no intervention on the waves themselves. Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2049.md) | Tandon and colleagues show that a sliding-window Transformer which keeps training on its context by next-token prediction at test time, from an initialization meta-learned for its loss after those updates, matches full attention's improvement in language-modelling loss with context length up to 128K at 3B parameters with constant per-token latency, while losing to full attention on verbatim retrieval, and that without the meta-learned initialization the test-time updates add little | From the reading of [LIT-2801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2801.md) in [NOTE-2087](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2087.md). Tandon, Dalal, Li, Koceja, Rød, ... and Sun (2025), arXiv 2512.23675. A sliding-window Transformer keeps learning at test time by next-token prediction on its context, compressing it into the MLP weights of its last quarter of blocks, from an initialization meta-learned for the loss after those updates. At 3B parameters it keeps full attention's scaling of loss with context length to 128K at constant per-token latency (2.7× faster at 128K), but loses to full attention on needle-in-a-haystack recall, and training is 3.4× slower at 8K. Here because A58 cited it for the owner's U26 case: its per-sequence weights and meta-learned initialization separate signal from interpreter ([CLAIM-118](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-118.md)), it prices work moved from inference into training ([QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md)), and its finding that test-time updates on an ordinarily trained model add little bears on the TTT arm of [CASE-294](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-294.md). Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2050.md) | Akyürek and colleagues show that transformers trained from scratch to do linear regression in context behave like standard estimators chosen by their capacity and the data: deep, wide ones match least squares on noiseless data and the Bayes-optimal ridge predictor under label noise, while one-layer models are closest to a single gradient step and two- to four-layer ones to ridge regression; the least-squares weights and moment vector can be decoded, nonlinearly, from their hidden states | From the reading of [LIT-2811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2811.md) in [NOTE-2121](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2121.md). Akyürek, Schuurmans, Andreas, Ma and Zhou (ICLR 2023; arXiv 2211.15661) prove that a transformer can implement one gradient-descent step or one ridge- regression update on in-context examples. They then show that transformers trained on in-context linear regression behave like standard estimators chosen by capacity: one gradient step at one layer (poorly), ridge at two to four layers, least squares at eight or more. With label noise the high-capacity learners match the Bayes-optimal ridge predictor. Probes recover the moment vector and least-squares weights from hidden states, but nonlinearly, unlike the constructions. Here because A56 cited it beside Garg et al. for in-context learning as a learned learner. It measures [THEORY-169](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-169.md)'s caution that trained transformers are not shown to do gradient descent, and it is a case of [CLAIM-118](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-118.md)'s split. Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2051.md) | Iqbal and colleagues show, at initialisation and large width and in experiments, that a deep network with U(1)- or O(k)-equivariant middle layers has a transition at σ_W = 1 above which a symmetry-broken phase conserves the relative phase of two inputs across layers and keeps one Jacobian component O(1) at any depth, so very deep networks train without normalisation over the whole phase, while the same order parameter in non-equivariant networks brings no gain | Iqbal, Keller, Song, Miyato and Welling ([LIT-2840](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2840.md)), read in [NOTE-2126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2126.md). A mean-field analysis gives the transition and the protected Jacobian component; 100-layer equivariant MLPs train across the broken phase; generic networks show the same order parameter with no performance gain. Defects (U(1) vortices) form in a convolutional RNN but their use is not shown. A stand-in for the thesis of [LIT-2787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2787.md), the owner's U6 example. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2052](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2052.md) | Garg and colleagues show that a transformer trained from scratch on prompts of input–output pairs from a simple function class learns unseen functions of that class in context about as well as the standard estimator: least squares for linear functions, near Lasso for sparse ones, better than greedy learning and boosting for depth-4 decision trees, and like a gradient-trained network for two-layer ReLU networks, and on linear functions it tracks least squares under several shifts of the prompt distribution | From the reading of [LIT-2839](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2839.md) in [NOTE-2103](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2103.md). Garg, Tsipras, Liang and Valiant (2022; arXiv 2208.01066, v3 Aug 2023) define in-context learning of a function class as a property of a fixed model and train small transformers from scratch to achieve it. On unseen 20-dimensional linear functions the trained model matches least squares, and it stays close under noisy labels, subspace inputs and mismatched orthants. Trained on sparse linear functions, depth-4 trees or two-layer networks, it nears Lasso, beats greedy tree learning and XGBoost, and matches a gradient-trained network. It is fragile under input scaling and skewed covariance, and the authors leave open what this means for language models. Here because A56 cited it for in-context learning as a learned algorithm. It is the behavioural counterpart to the exact identities of [THEORY-169](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-169.md) and a case of [CLAIM-118](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-118.md)'s split between a learned interpreter and a discarded per-sequence fit. Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-2055](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2055.md) | Velarde, Parra, Hashemi and Makse show that in layered networks a covering partition of units, units with equal colour-summed input and output weights, can only coarsen under gradient descent, and report that tolerance-defined quasi-covers grow during training of an MLP, a CNN and an LSTM agent and allow compression to 17–18% of size with little loss, while exact automorphisms are never observed | From the reading of [LIT-2843](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2843.md) in [NOTE-2085](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2085.md). Velarde, Parra, Hashemi and Makse (2026), arXiv 2609.01768 (v1, not peer reviewed). They carry graph fibrations to weighted layered networks as balanced colourings of units. They prove that a covering partition (equal colour- summed input and output weights) can only coarsen under gradient descent, and report that tolerance-defined quasi-covers grow during training of an MLP, a CNN and an LSTM agent, allowing compression to 17–18% of size; transformers are shown compressed, not tracked in training. Fibers here are computed with every input coordinate its own colour, so they are input-independent redundancies, not quotients of inputs, and the paper has no relational or rule task. Here because it is the evidence on the fibration side of the owner's U9 hunch, QUESTION- tmpex36a: it shows that balanced structure among units is learned without symmetry forcing it, and is silent on role abstraction. Read in its NOTE. | Proposed |
